summary.text: Assuming the first claimed identity, the shifted sequence \(u_k=a_{3773+k}+1\) obeys the Fibonacci recurrence modulo \(p=195318521017\); a modular computation from the initial terms gives \(u_k=u_{k+1}=1\) at \(k=249580073233\), so \(p\) divides two consecutive original terms. Their gcd \(g\) and the quotient \(q=(a_{3774+k}+a_{3773+k})/g\) are both at least \(2\), while the assumed identity and defining recurrence force \(g+q=1+gq\), an impossibility.

full_proof.text:
Let \((a_n)_{n\ge 1}\) be defined by
\[
a_1=a_2=1,
\qquad
a_n=g_n+\frac{a_{n-1}+a_{n-2}}{g_n}
\quad(n\ge3),
\]
where
\[
g_n=\gcd(a_{n-1},a_{n-2}).
\]
We prove that the conjecture is false. In fact, it is enough to disprove the first of its three asserted identities,
\[
a_n=1+a_{n-1}+a_{n-2}\qquad(n\ge3775), \tag{1}
\]
because the conjecture claims that all three identities hold for every such \(n\).

Assume, for a contradiction, that (1) holds for every \(n\ge3775\). Thus, for every integer \(k\ge0\),
\[
a_{3775+k}=1+a_{3774+k}+a_{3773+k}. \tag{2}
\]
We will derive a contradiction at the explicit shift
\[
k_0=249580073233.
\]
The corresponding index in the original sequence is
\[
3775+k_0=249580077008.
\]
The argument does not require direct computation of all sequence terms up to that enormous index. Instead, assumption (2) forces a Fibonacci recurrence, which can be studied modulo a suitable integer.

Define the shifted sequence
\[
b_k=a_{3773+k}+1 \qquad(k\ge0).
\]
Using (2), we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
b_{k+2}
 &=a_{3775+k}+1\\
 &=\bigl(1+a_{3774+k}+a_{3773+k}\bigr)+1\\
 &=\bigl(a_{3774+k}+1\bigr)+\bigl(a_{3773+k}+1\bigr)\\
 &=b_{k+1}+b_k.
\end{aligned} \tag{3}
\]
Thus, under the conjectural identity, \((b_k)\) is a Fibonacci-like sequence.

We use the modulus
\[
p=195318521017.
\]
Primality of \(p\) is not needed for the argument; all that is used is arithmetic modulo \(p\).

First we determine the two initial values needed for (3). A finite iteration of the defining recurrence gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{3773}={}&,\\
a_{3774}={}&.
\end{aligned} \tag{4}
\]
For completeness, this finite computation can be organized without ambiguity as follows. Starting with the pair
\[
P_0=(1,1),
\]
replace each pair \((r,s)\) by
\[
P_{j+1}=\left(s,\,\gcd(s,r)+\frac{s+r}{\gcd(s,r)}\right).
\]
An immediate induction on \(j\) shows that
\[
P_j=(a_{j+1},a_{j+2}).
\]
Performing these integer gcd, addition, and division operations for \(j=0,\ldots,3771\) yields (4). Only the residues modulo \(p\) will be needed below; division is performed in the integers during this finite recurrence computation, before reducing the resulting values modulo \(p\). Reducing (4) gives
\[
a_{3773}\equiv77940394258\pmod p,
\qquad
a_{3774}\equiv99768150821\pmod p. \tag{5}
\]
Consequently,
\[
b_0\equiv77940394259\pmod p,
\qquad
b_1\equiv99768150822\pmod p, \tag{6}
\]
and hence
\[
b_1-b_0\equiv21827756563\pmod p. \tag{7}
\]

Let \(F_0=0,F_1=1\), and \(F_{m+2}=F_{m+1}+F_m\) be the Fibonacci numbers. Every sequence satisfying (3) has the closed form
\[
b_k=b_0F_{k+1}+(b_1-b_0)F_k. \tag{8}
\]
This identity is valid over the integers and therefore also modulo \(p\). To prove it directly, at \(k=0\) its right side is \(b_0F_1+(b_1-b_0)F_0=b_0\), and at \(k=1\) it is \(b_0F_2+(b_1-b_0)F_1=b_1\). Thereafter both sides satisfy the same recurrence \(x_{k+2}=x_{k+1}+x_k\), so induction proves (8) for every \(k\).

We now need only three Fibonacci residues. A binary fast-doubling computation gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
F_{k_0}&\equiv21827756563\pmod p,\\
F_{k_0+1}&\equiv139205883321\pmod p,\\
F_{k_0+2}&\equiv161033639884\pmod p.
\end{aligned} \tag{9}
\]
Here is a precise description of this modular computation. The binary expansion used is
\[
k_0=(11101000011100001000011011000100010001)_2.
\]
Starting from \((F_0,F_1)=(0,1)\), process its binary digits using the standard doubling identities
\[
F_{2m}=F_m\bigl(2F_{m+1}-F_m\bigr),
\qquad
F_{2m+1}=F_m^2+F_{m+1}^2. \tag{10}
\]
If the next binary digit is \(0\), the new pair is \((F_{2m},F_{2m+1})\); if it is \(1\), the new pair is
\[
(F_{2m+1},F_{2m+2})=(F_{2m+1},F_{2m}+F_{2m+1}).
\]
Reducing after each multiplication and addition modulo \(195318521017\) produces
\[
(F_{k_0},F_{k_0+1})
 \equiv(21827756563,139205883321)\pmod p.
\]
The last residue in (9) is then the sum of these two residues modulo \(p\):
\[
21827756563+139205883321=161033639884<p.
\]
The identities in (10), which follow from the Fibonacci addition formula, also show inductively that this binary computation indeed returns the indicated Fibonacci residues.

Substitute (6), (7), and (9) into (8). At \(k=k_0\), we find
\[
\begin{aligned}
b_{k_0}
&\equiv77940394259\cdot139205883321
 +21827756563\cdot21827756563\\
&=11326212385784681827108\\
&=1+57988419771\cdot195318521017\\
&\equiv1\pmod p. 
\end{aligned} \tag{11}
\]
Similarly, at \(k=k_0+1\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
b_{k_0+1}
&\equiv77940394259\cdot161033639884
 +21827756563\cdot139205883321\\
&=15589577514788957011679\\
&=1+79816176334\cdot195318521017\\
&\equiv1\pmod p.
\end{aligned} \tag{12}
\]
Because \(b_k=a_{3773+k}+1\), congruences (11) and (12) imply
\[
a_{3773+k_0}\equiv0\pmod p,
\qquad
a_{3774+k_0}\equiv0\pmod p. \tag{13}
\]
Thus \(p\) divides two consecutive terms of the original sequence.

Set
\[
y=a_{3773+k_0},
\qquad x=a_{3774+k_0},
\qquad g=\gcd(x,y).
\]
Equation (13) implies
\[
p\mid g. \tag{14}
\]
We also need to know that \(x\) and \(y\) are positive. This already follows generally by induction from the defining recurrence, starting with \(a_1=a_2=1\). Alternatively, it follows immediately from our assumption (2): applying (2) with \(k=k_0-1\) expresses \(x=a_{3775+(k_0-1)}\) as \(1\) plus two nonnegative integers, while applying it with \(k=k_0-2\) does the same for \(y=a_{3775+(k_0-2)}\). Hence
\[
x\ge1,
\qquad y\ge1. \tag{15}
\]
In particular, \(g>0\). Since the positive integer \(g\) is divisible by \(p=195318521017\), (14) gives
\[
g\ge p\ge2. \tag{16}
\]

Now consider the very next term
\[
a_{3775+k_0}=a_{249580077008}.
\]
The defining recurrence says
\[
a_{3775+k_0}=g+\frac{x+y}{g}. \tag{17}
\]
On the other hand, the assumed identity (2), at \(k=k_0\), says
\[
a_{3775+k_0}=1+x+y. \tag{18}
\]
Let
\[
q=\frac{x+y}{g}.
\]
Because \(g\) divides both \(x\) and \(y\), write
\[
x=gr,
\qquad y=gs
\]
for nonnegative integers \(r,s\). By (15), \(x,y>0\), and since \(g>0\), this forces \(r,s\ge1\). Therefore
\[
q=r+s\ge2, \tag{19}
\]
and
\[
x+y=gq. \tag{20}
\]
Equating (17) and (18), and then using (20), gives
\[
g+q=1+gq. \tag{21}
\]
But (21) is impossible when \(g,q\ge2\). Indeed, rearranging it gives
\[
(g-1)(q-1)=gq-g-q+1=0,
\]
whereas both \(g-1\) and \(q-1\) are positive by (16) and (19).

This contradiction proves that (1) cannot hold for every \(n\ge3775\). Logically, if it fails at some index before \(249580077008\), the conjecture is already false; if it were to hold at every index through the construction above, the modular argument forces two consecutive terms to have a common divisor at least \(p\), and then it necessarily fails at \(n=249580077008\). In either case there is an \(n\ge3775\) for which the first asserted formula fails. Therefore the conjunction of all three formulas in the OEIS conjecture is false.
